title: Long Division With Remainders for Grade 4 (DMSB Made Simple) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Long Division With Remainders Grade 4 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach long division with remainders in Grade 4 using the divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down cycle, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: The long-division box scares more Grade 4 kids than any other page in the maths book. Here is the divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down cycle in plain words, why the remainder must stay small, and a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 674 ÷ 5 on the board and watch a Grade 4 class freeze. It is not the numbers that scare them — most can already share 20 sweets among 4 friends in their heads. It is the tall box, the digits stacked in columns, and the nagging worry about what to do with the bit left over. That leftover is the whole point of this lesson. Long division with remainders in Grade 4 is really just one four-step cycle, repeated calmly down the number, and once a child trusts the cycle the fear goes away.

The cycle has a name worth drilling until it is automatic: DMSB — Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Say it out loud. Chant it. I have taught nine-year-olds who could not tell me what 63 ÷ 7 was but who could rattle off ‘divide, multiply, subtract, bring down’ on demand, and that rhythm is what carries them through a three-digit dividend without losing their place.

What the remainder actually means

Before the algorithm, the idea. A remainder is simply what is left when a number cannot be shared out evenly. Share 17 pencils among 5 children: each gets 3, and 2 pencils sit on the table. We write that as 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, usually shortened to 3 R 2.

Here is the rule children must never break: the remainder is always smaller than the divisor. If you are dividing by 5 and you end up with a remainder of 6, you have made a mistake — another whole 5 could still have been shared out. In my experience this single check catches more errors than any other. A remainder of 5 when dividing by 5? Impossible. Go back.

The DMSB cycle, step by step

Let us work 674 ÷ 5 together. Set it out in the long-division box with 674 inside and 5 outside. Now run the cycle, one digit at a time, left to right.

StepWhat you do674 ÷ 5 in action
DivideHow many times does 5 go into the digit?5 into 6 goes 1 time → write 1 on top
MultiplyMultiply that answer by the divisor1 × 5 = 5, write it under the 6
SubtractTake it away to find what is left6 − 5 = 1
Bring downPull down the next digit beside the remainderbring down 7 → you now have 17

Then repeat. 5 into 17 goes 3 times (3 × 5 = 15), 17 − 15 = 2, bring down the 4 to make 24. 5 into 24 goes 4 times (4 × 5 = 20), 24 − 20 = 4, and there is no digit left to bring down. So 674 ÷ 5 = 134 remainder 4. Notice the final leftover, 4, is smaller than 5 — exactly as it should be.

The zero that trips everyone up

The most common Grade 4 slip is dropping a digit instead of writing a zero. Take 618 ÷ 6. Six goes into 6 once, subtract to get 0, bring down the 1 — and now 6 into 1 goes zero times. That zero must be written on top, or the answer collapses from 103 to a wrong 13. Tell your child: if you bring a digit down and the divisor will not go into it, you still write a 0 and carry on. Never skip a column.

Checking the answer — the reverse test

Every long division can be checked with one tidy formula, and I insist my students use it every single time:

  • quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend
  • For 674 ÷ 5 = 134 R 4: 134 × 5 = 670, then 670 + 4 = 674. It matches, so the answer is correct.
  • If the total does not land back on the original number, something in the cycle went wrong — usually a subtraction slip or a forgotten zero.

This check does something quietly powerful: it turns division back into multiplication, the operation your child is already more confident with, and it makes them the one who confirms their own work instead of waiting for a tick from the teacher.

A worked example with a stubborn remainder

Try 857 ÷ 4. Four into 8 is 2 (2 × 4 = 8, subtract 0), bring down 5. Four into 5 is 1 (1 × 4 = 4), 5 − 4 = 1, bring down 7 to make 17. Four into 17 is 4 (4 × 4 = 16), 17 − 16 = 1. Answer: 214 remainder 1. Check: 214 × 4 = 856, plus 1 = 857. Perfect. The remainder 1 is smaller than the divisor 4, so we are safe.

Little habits that prevent big mistakes

  • Line up the digits in neat columns — squared paper is worth its weight in gold for this topic.
  • Say ‘divide, multiply, subtract, bring down’ aloud for the first week; the words stop children skipping the subtraction.
  • Estimate first. 674 ÷ 5 is roughly 700 ÷ 5 = 140, so an answer near 134 feels right and a wild answer like 34 obviously does not.
  • Always run the reverse check before moving on.

One honest caveat: do not rush a child onto three-digit dividends until the two-digit ones are boringly easy. Fluency with 68 ÷ 4 first, then 674 ÷ 5. Speed is the last thing to arrive, not the first.

Test the DMSB cycle below

Here is a short, free quiz on exactly what we covered — the divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down cycle, remainders, the zero trap, and the reverse check. Let your child work each one on paper first, then read the explanations for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 4 Long Division With Remainders Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the DMSB cycle, remainders and the reverse check. Work each one on paper, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 4 long division of 2 to 3 digit numbers by a 1-digit divisor

questions.explanation: 5 goes into 47 nine times (9 × 5 = 45), and 47 − 45 = 2. So the answer is 9 remainder 2.

questions.q: In the DMSB cycle, what does the letter S stand for?
questions.explanation: DMSB is Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. The S is Subtract — you take away to find what is left.

questions.q: When you divide a number by 6, which of these can NEVER be the remainder?
questions.explanation: The remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. Dividing by 6, the remainder can be 0 to 5, so 7 is impossible.
6 into 6 is 1, 6 into 1 is 0 (write the zero!), 6 into 18 is 3. The answer is 103, not 13.

questions.q: You work out 96 ÷ 7 = 13 remainder 5. Which check confirms it?
questions.explanation: The check is quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend. 13 × 7 = 91, plus 5 = 96. It matches.
8 into 72 is 9, 8 into 5 is 0 (write the zero), leaving 5. So 725 ÷ 8 = 90 remainder 5.

questions.q: After you subtract in one step, what do you do next in the cycle?
questions.explanation: After Subtract comes Bring down: pull the next digit beside the leftover, then start Divide again.
4 into 8 is 2, 4 into 9 is 2 (2 × 4 = 8), leaving 1. So 89 ÷ 4 = 22 remainder 1, and 1 is smaller than 4.

faq.q: What does DMSB stand for in long division?
faq.a: It is the four-step cycle you repeat down the number: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Chanting it aloud stops children skipping the subtraction step.

faq.q: Why must the remainder be smaller than the divisor?
faq.a: Because if the leftover is as big as the divisor, another whole group could still be shared out. Dividing by 5, a remainder of 5 or more means you divided incorrectly — go back and check.

faq.q: How do I check a long division answer?
faq.a: Use quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend. For 47 ÷ 5 = 9 R 2, work out 9 × 5 = 45, then 45 + 2 = 47. If it lands back on the original number, the answer is right.

faq.q: What is the most common Grade 4 long-division mistake?
faq.a: Forgetting to write a zero in the quotient when the divisor will not go into a brought-down digit. That single slip turns 618 ÷ 6 = 103 into a wrong 13. Never skip a column.
